chapter: Washington in the 1930s: big bands, lessons, first jobs
title: A future brother-in-law who plays fast chromatics, and George McIver
summary: Neighborhood friends, a pianist whose sister studied at Howard and the music-loving George McIver with his kazoo.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: I guess from there, somewhere in the interim of all of this, was when I began to play...to listen a lot more. In the meantime, I was sort of approaching the high school age and just getting involved with this music more and more. When I was about 15 years old, well even before then, in the neighborhood, there was a fellow who later became my brother-in-law -- he was about a year older than I. And he played the piano. His sister was a music major at Howard University then. Some things that he had learned that I never will forget... One of the main things that he did that fascinated me was that he played chromatics very fast. I thought that was really great, because I hadn't gotten to that stage where I was playing the chromatic scale. He used to play things,
make these little runs up and down the piano. So he and I became fast friends, and we used to sit down and play the piano at my house or his house.

Then along with him, a guy that at that particular time I used to play football with around a lot, whose name was George McIver. And like my mother, and so many people I've met since then that have this I don't know what you'd call it... They have this knack for knowing music, and they never play an instrument, they never studied music or anything, but there's a love that they have for it that just makes them knowledgeable about music beyond a lot of musicians that I've known who studied. In other words, these people to me are better musicians than some of the musicians that I've known! And every now and then, I run across a person like that.

My mother was certainly one of those people, and this fellow George McIver was that kind of a guy. He used to like to tap dance, and he used to like to buy a gift of these horns... We used to call them the kazoo. It's a little thing where you put a piece of paper... There's a little horn, and you put a piece of paper in it (you could do the same thing with a comb) and hum through it and make these sounds. So I would sit and play the piano, and he'd sit beside me, and we'd just have a ball in my living room doing these things.
